WHITLOCK & DEENE LLP — INTERNAL RULE MEMORANDUM (Evidence Practice Group)
Re: Applying the hearsay definition in trial preparation

Section 1. The rule. Hearsay is an out-of-court statement offered in evidence to prove the truth of the matter asserted in the statement. Both elements are required: (a) the statement must have been made outside the current trial or hearing, and (b) the proponent must be offering it to prove that its content is true. If either element is missing, the item is not hearsay and this memo's test is not satisfied.

Section 2. What counts as a 'statement.' A statement is (i) an oral assertion, (ii) a written assertion, or (iii) nonverbal conduct of a person, if the person intended the conduct as an assertion. The firm's settled position, which associates must apply without deviation: a nod, a headshake, or pointing in direct response to a question is nonverbal conduct intended as an assertion and is therefore a statement. If such conduct occurred out of court and is offered to prove the truth of what it asserted, it IS hearsay. By contrast, conduct not intended to communicate anything — for example, a person putting up an umbrella, or an athlete's record time in a race — is not a statement at all and can never be hearsay.

Section 3. Common non-hearsay purposes. An out-of-court statement is NOT hearsay when offered for a purpose other than its truth, including: (a) effect on the listener — to show that the hearer was on notice, was warned, or had a motive, regardless of whether the statement was accurate; (b) verbal acts — words with independent legal significance, such as the words of offer, acceptance, or defamation; (c) impeachment — to show a witness said something inconsistent, not that the earlier statement was true; (d) circumstantial evidence of the declarant's state of mind. Live, in-court testimony given by a witness on the stand at the current proceeding is likewise not hearsay, even if elicited on cross-examination.

Section 4. Application discipline. Identify (1) the declarant, (2) where the statement was made, and (3) the precise purpose stated by the proponent. When our client letter states the purpose for which an item will be offered, take that stated purpose as controlling; do not invent an alternative purpose. If the stated purpose is to prove the truth of the matter asserted and the statement was made out of court, the hearsay test is satisfied. If the stated purpose is notice or another listed non-truth purpose, the test is not satisfied even for an identical statement.

This memo controls over any earlier evidence-practice drafts circulated before this fiscal year.

WHITLOCK & DEENE LLP — INTERNAL RULE MEMORANDUM (Civil Procedure Group)
Re: Forum-selection screening: personal jurisdiction and diversity jurisdiction

PART I — PERSONAL JURISDICTION.
A forum state has personal jurisdiction over a defendant in either of two ways.
(1) General jurisdiction: the defendant is domiciled in the forum state. An individual is domiciled where they reside with intent to remain; a corporation is at home in its state of incorporation and the state of its principal place of business.
(2) Specific jurisdiction: BOTH prongs below must be satisfied —
  (a) Purposeful contacts: the defendant has sufficient contacts with the forum such that it has purposefully availed itself of the privileges of conducting activities there. Contacts created unilaterally by the plaintiff, and merely fortuitous presence such as passing through the state in transit on unrelated business, do not count.
  (b) Nexus: the plaintiff's claim arises out of or relates to those forum contacts.
Firm rule of decision: if the defendant is not domiciled in the forum and either prong (a) or prong (b) fails, personal jurisdiction is lacking. A defendant who repeatedly traveled into the forum to solicit and negotiate the very contract being sued upon satisfies both prongs. A defendant with no operations, customers, or purposeful activity in the forum — whose only connection is unrelated transit — satisfies neither.

PART II — DIVERSITY JURISDICTION.
A federal court has diversity jurisdiction when BOTH requirements are met:
(1) Complete diversity: no plaintiff is a citizen of the same state as any defendant. A corporation is a citizen of every state where it is incorporated AND the state of its principal place of business.
(2) Amount in controversy: the amount in controversy must EXCEED $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs. The firm's settled position, adopted after the Calloway remand: a demand of exactly $75,000.00 does NOT satisfy the requirement, because the statute requires that the matter in controversy exceed the sum of $75,000. Associates must not round in the client's favor; exactly $75,000 fails.
Both requirements are independent. Complete diversity with an insufficient amount fails; a large amount without complete diversity fails.

PART III — WORKFLOW. When screening an intake letter, resolve each numbered scenario separately, apply only the tests above, and record one determination per scenario. This memo supersedes all earlier jurisdiction threshold drafts, including any draft referencing a $50,000 threshold or a 'doing business' test; those drafts are withdrawn and must not be cited.

WHITLOCK & DEENE LLP — INTERNAL RULE MEMORANDUM (Commercial Group)
Re: Determining whether a contract is governed by UCC Article 2 or by the common law

Section 1. The rule. UCC Article 2 governs contracts for the sale of goods. Goods are movable, tangible things — canned food, machinery, vehicles, packaging, grain. The common law governs contracts for services, real estate, employment, construction on land, and intangibles such as intellectual property licenses. The classification question is purely about subject matter, not about price, sophistication of the parties, or whether the deal was written.

Section 2. Clean cases. A contract whose entire subject is the transfer of title to identified movable tangible items for a price is governed by Article 2. A contract whose entire subject is the performance of labor, consulting, design, or advisory work is governed by the common law, even when the service provider incidentally uses or delivers paper, software printouts, or other trivial materials while performing.

Section 3. Hybrid contracts — predominant purpose test. Many contracts mix goods and services (equipment plus installation; software plus training; food supply plus delivery staffing). For hybrid contracts the firm applies the predominant purpose test: classify the contract according to its dominant thrust. Our operational rule, which associates must apply mechanically when the letter supplies a price allocation: if MORE THAN HALF of the total contract price is attributable to the goods component, the ENTIRE contract is governed by UCC Article 2; if half or more of the price is attributable to services, the entire contract is governed by the common law. Do not split a single contract into two regimes.

Section 4. Vocabulary for the file. When recording a scope determination in the matter system, the firm uses a binary vocabulary: a determination that Article 2 governs is recorded as the affirmative disposition; a determination that the common law governs is recorded as the negative disposition. The recording clerk's instructions in each assignment control the exact strings.

Section 5. Traps to avoid. (a) The presence of a large dollar figure does not make a services contract a goods contract. (b) Installation and training obligations do not remove an equipment sale from Article 2 when the price allocation shows the goods predominate. (c) Real estate purchases are never Article 2 transactions regardless of what sits on the land. Questions on this memo go to the Commercial Group knowledge partner.

WHITLOCK & DEENE LLP — INTERNAL RULE MEMORANDUM (M&A / Litigation Interface Group)
Re: Successor liability screening for asset acquisitions

Section 1. The general rule. When one company purchases the assets of another, the purchaser is generally NOT liable for the seller's debts and liabilities. Asset deals are therefore the default structure for liability containment. The general rule yields only where one of four recognized exceptions applies.

Section 2. The four exceptions.
(1) Express agreement: the purchaser expressly agrees in the transaction documents to assume the seller's liabilities. An assumption clause covering the relevant class of liabilities is sufficient by itself; no other factor is needed.
(2) Fraudulent conveyance: the assets are transferred to the purchaser in order to escape liability — indicators include inadequate consideration, a seller left insolvent and unable to satisfy known claims, and awareness of looming claims coupled with a structure designed to strand them.
(3) De facto merger: the transaction is a merger in substance — continuity of ownership between seller shareholders and purchaser, cessation and dissolution of the seller, assumption by the purchaser of the operations needed to continue the business, and continuity of management.
(4) Mere continuation: the purchaser is the same enterprise wearing a new coat — common officers, directors, or shareholders, and only one corporation remaining after the transfer.

Section 3. What is NOT an exception. The firm's settled screening positions: (a) the purchaser's mere knowledge of the seller's potential liabilities, without more, triggers no exception; (b) payment of fair market value in an arm's-length sale negates the fraudulent conveyance indicators; (c) where the seller corporation survives the closing, retains its separate existence, and applies the sale proceeds to its creditors, neither de facto merger nor mere continuation is available; (d) absence of any shared officers, directors, or shareholders defeats mere continuation. A transaction bearing all of features (b), (c), and (d), with no assumption clause, falls under the general rule: the purchaser takes free of the seller's liabilities.

Section 4. Recording discipline. Screening determinations are recorded per scenario in the matter system. A determination that at least one exception applies (successor exposure attaches) is the affirmative disposition; a determination that the general rule controls (no exception applies) is the negative disposition. The assignment instructions control the exact recording strings. Always name the operative exception, if any, in your rationale.

WHITLOCK & DEENE LLP — INTERNAL RULE MEMORANDUM (Brands & Trademark Group)
Re: Classifying marks on the Abercrombie spectrum during clearance

Section 1. The five categories. Every candidate mark is classified into exactly one of five categories, listed from weakest to strongest:
(1) generic — the mark is the common name for the product or service itself. The word answers the question 'what is it?' (e.g., the word for the product category used as the brand of that very product). Generic terms receive no protection.
(2) descriptive — the mark directly describes a purpose, nature, attribute, feature, quality, or characteristic of the product. No mental leap is required: the consumer reads the mark and immediately understands, without imagination, a fact about the product. Descriptive marks are protectable only with secondary meaning.
(3) suggestive — the mark suggests or implies a quality or characteristic, requiring the consumer to exercise imagination, thought, or a multi-step inference to connect the mark to the product's attributes. The dividing line from descriptive: if the mark states the attribute directly, it is descriptive; if the consumer must reason through an association to reach the attribute, it is suggestive.
(4) arbitrary — the mark is a real, existing word (a word found in the dictionary or in ordinary usage) that has NO relation to the product it brands.
(5) fanciful — the mark is an invented or coined word: a term with no prior meaning in any language, created for the purpose of serving as a mark.

Section 2. Firm classification discipline. Apply the categories in this order of inquiry. First ask whether the term exists as a word at all: an invented term with no dictionary meaning is fanciful — it can never be arbitrary, because arbitrary status is reserved for real words. If the term is a real word or a readable combination of real words, ask what it communicates about the product: the common name is generic; a direct statement of an attribute the product actually has is descriptive; an indirect implication requiring imagination is suggestive; no relation at all is arbitrary.

Section 3. Recording. Clearance determinations are logged as evidence records on the client matter, one record per mark, with the category slug in lowercase exactly as written in Section 1: generic, descriptive, suggestive, arbitrary, fanciful. The assignment instructions state where each record is filed. When the client's letter recites why a name was chosen and what the product's actual features are, treat those recitals as established facts for classification purposes.

MERIDIAN GRAIN COOPERATIVE
Office of the General Counsel — Dorrance, Kansas

To our trial team at Whitlock & Deene LLP:

As we prepare for trial in the north silo fire case (Meridian Grain Cooperative v. Aldermoor Fan & Blower Co.), please screen the following three evidentiary items. For each, we state exactly what the item is and the precise purpose for which we intend to offer it. Please analyze each scenario separately under the firm's evidence memo.

SCENARIO A. To prove that the north silo exhaust fan was in fact defective, we intend to have warehouse worker Tobias Prell testify that, on the day after the fire, foreman Della Kite told him: 'the north silo fan has been shorting for weeks.' Ms. Kite made this remark in the loading yard, not in any court proceeding. Our purpose in offering the remark is to prove that the fan really had been shorting — that is, to prove the truth of what Ms. Kite said.

SCENARIO B. Separately, to prove that Aldermoor's regional operations manager, Petra Vosniak, was on notice of a possible defect two weeks before the fire, we intend to show that Ms. Kite made the very same remark — 'the north silo fan has been shorting for weeks' — directly to Ms. Vosniak at the February vendor meeting. For this item, we do not care whether the remark was accurate. Our sole stated purpose is to show the effect on the listener: that having heard the warning, Ms. Vosniak was on notice and had a duty to inspect. We are NOT offering this item to prove the fan was actually shorting.

SCENARIO C. Fire investigator Ruth Ohanian interviewed night watchman Arno Besh at the scene. Mr. Besh could not speak due to smoke inhalation. Investigator Ohanian asked him directly: 'Did you see the fan spark before the flames started?' Mr. Besh looked at her and deliberately nodded his head in response to the question. We intend to offer testimony about the nod to prove that the fan did spark before the flames started — that is, to prove the truth of what Mr. Besh communicated by nodding. The nod occurred at the fire scene, out of court.

Please record one determination per scenario as your engagement instructions direct, and note that our statements above about the purpose of each offer are final; the trial committee has locked them.

Very truly yours,
Halima Droste, General Counsel
Meridian Grain Cooperative

OSTRANDER TOOLING WORKS, INC.
Canton, Ohio — Office of the President

To the Civil Procedure Group, Whitlock & Deene LLP:

Ostrander Tooling Works, Inc. is an Ohio corporation with its only plant and headquarters in Canton, Ohio; treat Ostrander as a citizen of Ohio and domiciled in Ohio for all scenarios. We have four forum questions. Please analyze each numbered scenario independently under the firm's jurisdiction memo and record one determination per scenario as your assignment directs.

SCENARIO 1 (personal jurisdiction — proposed suit in Ohio). We wish to sue Karvella Presses LLC, an Indiana company with its principal place of business in Fort Wayne, Indiana, in an Ohio court for breach of our hydraulic press supply contract. The relevant history: Karvella's sales director traveled to Ohio six separate times over eight months to demonstrate press models on our Canton floor and to negotiate terms, and Karvella signed the supply contract at our Canton offices. The breach we would sue over is Karvella's failure to deliver the very presses ordered under that contract.

SCENARIO 2 (personal jurisdiction — proposed suit in Ohio). We also wish to sue Brumfeld Freight Lines, a Georgia carrier with its principal place of business in Savannah, Georgia, in an Ohio court over a loading-dock injury to our purchasing agent that occurred entirely at Brumfeld's Savannah terminal during a site visit. Brumfeld has no operations in Ohio, no Ohio customers, no Ohio employees, and solicits no business in Ohio. Its only connection to Ohio that our investigator could find: one Brumfeld driver once drove through Ohio in transit on a Pennsylvania-to-Kentucky route unrelated to our claim.

SCENARIO 3 (diversity jurisdiction — proposed federal suit). Ostrander (Ohio citizen, sole plaintiff) intends to sue Quenneville Alloys Inc., which is incorporated in Delaware and has its principal place of business in Louisville, Kentucky, as sole defendant, for supplying out-of-specification alloy stock. Our damages demand is $410,000, exclusive of interest and costs.

SCENARIO 4 (diversity jurisdiction — proposed federal suit). Ostrander (Ohio citizen, sole plaintiff) intends to sue Talwick Machining Corp., which is incorporated in Michigan and has its principal place of business in Lansing, Michigan, as sole defendant, over a rejected tooling order. Our accountants have fixed the damages demand at exactly $75,000.00, exclusive of interest and costs, and the board will not authorize pleading a higher figure.

With thanks,
Edwin Ostrander III, President

HALCYON PROVISIONS COMPANY
Providence, Rhode Island — Legal Operations

To the Commercial Group, Whitlock & Deene LLP:

Ahead of our annual audit we need a governing-law scoping determination — UCC Article 2 or common law — for three contracts in our active portfolio. Please analyze each contract separately under the firm's Article 2 scope memo and record one determination per contract as your assignment instructions direct. The recitals below are complete and accurate; no other terms bear on classification.

CONTRACT 1 — Bramblewick Orchards supply agreement. Halcyon agrees to purchase, and Bramblewick Orchards LLC agrees to sell and deliver, 1,200 cases of jarred stone-fruit preserves, packed to our label specification, for a total price of $86,400. Title to the cases passes to Halcyon on delivery at our Providence warehouse. The contract contains no service obligations of any kind beyond ordinary delivery of the cases.

CONTRACT 2 — Ferrand & Slate advisory engagement. Halcyon engages the consulting firm Ferrand & Slate Partners to study and redesign our warehouse picking workflow, deliver a written recommendations report, and coach our floor supervisors through implementation, for a professional fee of $54,000. Ferrand & Slate sells us no equipment and transfers title to nothing except the paper report embodying its advice. The entire subject of the engagement is advisory and design labor.

CONTRACT 3 — Marovic Equipment bottling line agreement. Halcyon agrees to buy a model MX-9 automated bottling line from Marovic Equipment Corp. for a single total contract price of $290,000. The contract itself allocates the price: $248,000 is attributable to the bottling line machinery (the goods component), and $42,000 is attributable to on-site installation, calibration, and operator training (the services component). It is a single indivisible contract; the parties did not execute separate agreements.

For the avoidance of doubt: Contract 1 involves no real estate; Contract 2 involves no transfer of goods beyond the report paper; Contract 3's allocation figures above are the ones our auditors have certified.

Regards,
Sybil Antczak, Director of Legal Operations
Halcyon Provisions Company

HALCYON PROVISIONS COMPANY
Providence, Rhode Island — Legal Operations

To the M&A and Brands teams, Whitlock & Deene LLP:

Two groups of questions from our expansion program. Please handle each numbered item independently under the applicable firm memo and record determinations as your assignment instructions direct.

PART ONE — SUCCESSOR LIABILITY SCREENING.

ACQUISITION 1 — Pellworth Canning. Two years ago Halcyon purchased substantially all of the assets of Pellworth Canning Co. Section 7.2 of the executed asset purchase agreement states that the purchaser 'expressly assumes all product liability obligations of Seller, whether arising before or after Closing.' A consumer class has now sued Halcyon over defective seams in cans Pellworth manufactured before the closing — squarely a product liability claim of the seller. We need a determination whether successor exposure attaches to Halcyon for this claim.

ACQUISITION 2 — Dunlow Cold Storage. Last year Halcyon purchased the warehouse racking, refrigeration units, and delivery fleet of Dunlow Cold Storage LLC in an arm's-length sale at a price our banker certified as fair market value. The purchase agreement contains NO assumption of liabilities of any kind. Dunlow remained in existence after the closing, retained its corporate registration, and applied the sale proceeds to its creditors. No officer, director, or shareholder of Dunlow holds any position or share in Halcyon, and Halcyon has never held itself out as Dunlow. A vendor with an old unpaid invoice against Dunlow now demands payment from Halcyon. We need a determination whether successor exposure attaches to Halcyon for this claim.

PART TWO — BRAND CLEARANCE (Abercrombie classification).

MARK 1 — QUELLIVAR. Our agency coined the term QUELLIVAR for our new canned soup line. The term was invented from scratch for this project; it has no prior meaning in English or in any other language, appears in no dictionary, and was verified by the agency as a pure coinage with no existing usage anywhere.

MARK 2 — CRISPCRUST. For our frozen pizza line we propose the mark CRISPCRUST. The product's defining feature, confirmed by our test kitchen, is its notably crisp crust, and the name was chosen precisely because it directly states that feature to the shopper. A consumer reading the mark on the freezer door understands immediately, without any imagination or inference, that the pizza has a crisp crust.

Please log one determination for each acquisition and one classification record for each mark.

Regards,
Sybil Antczak, Director of Legal Operations
Halcyon Provisions Company

WHITLOCK & DEENE LLP — DRAFT MEMORANDUM (WITHDRAWN)
Status: SUPERSEDED. This draft was circulated for comment and formally withdrawn by the Civil Procedure Group. It is retained in the document store for records purposes only. Do not cite, apply, or rely on any statement in this draft. The operative guidance is the current firm rule memo on personal jurisdiction and diversity jurisdiction.

Draft Part A — Diversity thresholds (obsolete). This draft proposed screening diversity intakes against an amount-in-controversy threshold of $50,000, and further proposed that a demand of exactly the threshold amount should be treated as sufficient 'in the interest of client access to the federal forum.' Neither proposal was adopted. The comment process identified both as inconsistent with the governing statute, which requires that the matter in controversy exceed the current statutory sum. Associates who screened files against this draft between March and May were instructed to re-run their determinations.

Draft Part B — Personal jurisdiction (obsolete). This draft proposed a single-factor 'doing business' test under which any defendant who had ever transacted any business in the forum state, of any kind and at any time, would be subject to personal jurisdiction there for all claims. The comment process rejected this test as overbroad: it ignored the requirement that a claim arise out of or relate to the defendant's forum contacts, and it treated fortuitous or unrelated contacts as sufficient. The adopted rule instead requires purposeful contacts plus a nexus between the contacts and the claim, or domicile in the forum.

Draft Part C — Records note. Files screened under this draft carry the banner code CP-DRAFT-9. If you encounter a determination citing CP-DRAFT-9, flag it to the knowledge partner for re-screening under the operative memo. The withdrawal notice was circulated firm-wide, and the Civil Procedure Group's operative memo expressly supersedes this draft by name.

End of withdrawn draft. Retained unedited for the archive. For any live matter, consult the operative rule memoranda maintained by the practice groups, not this document.
